::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[show the sequence has the limit 0, $x_n$=$\frac{10^{3n}}{n!}$](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3127416/show-the-sequence-has-the-limit-0-x-n-frac103nn), asked by [user597188](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/643822/user597188) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2019-02-26; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> show the sequence has the limit 0, $x_n$=$\frac{10^{3n}}{n!}$ 
>
> I started with:
>
> $10^3$=1000 
>
> $x_1$=$\frac{10^{3(1)}}{1!}$=1000
>
> $x_2$=$\frac{10^{3(2)}}{2!}$=500000>$x_1$
>
> $x_3$=$\frac{10^{3(3)}}{3!}$=500000000/3>$x_2$
>
> .
>
> .
>
> .
>
> How do I show the limit actually does go to 0.
:::

The series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty x_n$ converges to $e^{10^3}$, so the sequence of terms in the series converge to zero.
